To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the DSCR is a region of about 34 kb on Hsa21, located on distal 22q13, and is a candidate to induce intellectual disability and some phenotypes of DS.
the minimal critical region for DS is 34 kb long, it contains no known gene, and it is absent in all healthy humans, but is present in all DS individuals.

(1) the HR-DSCR is a 34-kb region on 21 q 22.13, the smallest region of the Hsa21 genome whose duplication is sufficient and necessary to induce all DS constant phenotypes; (2) the HR-DSCRs are the only Hsa21 regions whose duplication is shared only by DS patients and absent in all non DS subjects; (3) HR-DSCR is also spared by any duplication copy number variant (CNV) in healthy subjects
In summary, our research is concerned with
a novel, systematic, comparative map of the PT21 cases, with a view to defining a DSCR, which is now restricted to a 34 kb region on 21 q22.13.
the identification of a critical genomic region in DS, which is the most significant finding in the last 40 years.
the identification of the genetic causes of DS and the development of new therapeutic strategies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the HR-DSCR is a critical region for DS, and the DSCR is the minimal region sufficient to induce the DS phenotype.
the DSCR, which is sufficient to induce the main phenotypes of DS, is located in the HR-DSCR, which is located in Hsa21q22.3.
the DS phenotype results from a complex interaction between the HR-DSCR and the rest of the human genome.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
DS is not a disease but rather a ‘genetic condition’, and that its most constant features may be explained by the duplication of a small region on distal 22q13.3.
the HR-DSCR is not the DSCR but it is the most critical region of Hsa21 for DS.
the DSCR is a small region, and the DSCR is not a gene.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the DS phenotype is likely to be caused by a small number of loci, each of which has a limited effect on the phenotype.
the DSCR is a small, highly restricted, and well-defined genomic interval, and that its study may provide important insights into the genotype–phenotype relationship in DS.
a small genomic region is responsible for most DS features and that the DS phenotype is not due to a simple gene dosage imbalance.
